variants.headline: A bargain with {{partner}}, and gold in the terms
body: Our envoys and {{partner}} have struck a bargain, and gold is written into it. We put up {{weGive}}; {{weGet}} comes back to us. At the wharf, a porter who had been paid in promises all month says he will believe in the bargain when the coin is in his hand.

variants.headline: A bargain abroad, with gold in the terms
body: A bargain has been struck with a foreign power, and gold is among its terms. We give {{weGive}} and take {{weGet}} in return. A carter who had kept his horses harnessed until the terms were settled now says he can send them home and rest them for a week.

variants.headline: The terms of the bargain
body: Out of our hands: {{weGive}}.
Into our hands: {{weGet}}.
Gold rides with these terms, and the clerk has left a line open for it in a thin book.

variants.headline: Hear it! Terms are struck with {{partner}}
body: Hear it, {{terms.civic.people}}! A bargain is struck with {{partner}}! We hand over {{weGive}}; {{weGet}} comes back to us; and gold is in the middle of it! Watch the market stalls this week, for prices move before the coin does!

variants.headline: The envoys earn their keep
body: Look at the terms, {{terms.civic.people}}: {{partner}} has signed, we give {{weGive}}, we take {{weGet}}, and gold seals it. Bargains like this are not made by speeches. Your {{terms.civic.government}} kept its envoys at the table until the page was signed, and the shops will feel the difference before the month is out.

variants.headline: A trade route bound for us is plundered
body: A caravan bound for our markets has been robbed on the road, and its goods will not arrive. At the market, a spice seller has chalked a shorter list on her board and told the customers waiting there to come back when the roads are quieter. The loss will show up in prices before it shows up in any report.

variants.headline: {{plunderer}} robs the road to our gates
body: {{plunderer}} took a caravan bound for our gates, and nothing of it will reach the market. The raiders chose their ground and their hour, which tells you they had watched the run before. A band that learns our roads once will not forget them.

variants.headline: Payday for the raiders
body: The gang that hit a caravan bound for us walked away with {{gold}} gold. At the unloading yard, a porter turned his slate face down and said he would not stand at the gate after dark for the old rate. His wife, he added, was already counting what the raid would cost them.

variants.headline: Trade needs a guarded road
body: A caravan meant for our merchants was stripped on the road, and the men who loaded it want to know what the {{terms.civic.government}} will do about the next one. We are told that escorts are costly and the roads are long, which is true and answers nothing. Either give the shippers guards or tell them plainly that the road is theirs to risk.

variants.headline: The road from {{origin}} is robbed
body: They say the caravan from {{origin}} never came in. Robbers met it on the road, and the drivers went home with empty carts and nothing to show for the season. The market here goes thin, the merchants there go quiet, and somewhere a band of thieves is drinking to a good week.

variants.headline: Our outgoing trade has stopped
body: The last road our merchants used for foreign trade is closed, and no caravan of ours sets out now. The goods that used to leave by that road stay behind in the warehouses. At the depot, the loading master has put his tally board away and told his crew to find other work.

variants.headline: The weights are put away
body: In this season the last road to a foreign market fell idle, and no caravan of ours travels that road now. It was a road that once carried our goods out and foreign coin back, and the yard that provisioned it is quiet. The keeper of the scales has wrapped the weights in cloth and closed the chest.

variants.headline: Small exporters have less room to wait
body: At the last reckoning {{routes}} outgoing trade routes stood open; this week not one does. A merchant with goods already packed has nowhere to send them, and the small workshop that cannot store a month of work will be the first to let a hand go. Whoever let the last road close owes those shops an account of why, and a date when a new one opens.

variants.headline: Notice to those who send trade out
body: Notice to shippers and warehousemen: no outgoing trade route remains open. Store what is made up for export, dry and counted, and take no new orders until a road is announced. The workshops keep working; the warehouses hold the goods.

variants.headline: Trade run complete between cities {{routeDistance}} apart
body: A caravan has completed the long road between {{ourCity}} and {{theirCity}}. The two cities stand {{routeDistance}} apart, and the goods arrived with the dust of the whole distance on them. At the customs shed, a clerk who logged the load says the merchants are already talking about a second run before the weather turns.

variants.headline: The next order from {{theirCity}}
body: Our merchants have carried a full load from {{ourCity}} to {{theirCity}} and come home with the road behind them. The opening is not the single cargo but the habit a second run would build: a buyer in {{theirCity}} could name a color and a measure and count on seeing both again. A workshop in {{ourCity}} that learns to fill such orders will have work booked before the cloth is woven.

variants.headline: A long road ends at {{ourCity}}
body: We are informed that a caravan from {{theirCity}} has finished the long road to {{ourCity}}, a journey of {{routeDistance}}. The carter, it is said, asked at the gate for nothing more than a trough and a night's lodging for his beasts. Our merchants would do well to remember him kindly, for a road stays open by the welcome it finds at both ends.

variants.headline: A trade run with {{partner}} enters the record
body: In this season a caravan finished the long road between {{theirCity}} and {{ourCity}}, and {{partner}} is named in the margin. The record notes the two cities, {{ourCity}} and {{theirCity}}, and the distance between them, {{routeDistance}}. The goods it carried are entered beneath, and the names of the merchants after.

variants.headline: A run of {{routeDistance}}, completed
body: {{ourCity}} and {{theirCity}}, {{routeDistance}}, done. The carts went home empty and the buyers are already asking when the next ones leave. Long road, good season.

variants.headline: Raiders cut short an outgoing trade route
body: A caravan that left our territory has been robbed on the road, and its cargo is lost. At the dispatch yard, a clerk spent the morning crossing names off a list and counting coins back into the hands of merchants who had paid for space. The next caravan will leave lighter, if it leaves at all.

variants.headline: {{plunderer}} takes our trade on the road
body: {{plunderer}} took our caravan on the road, and the goods in it will never reach a buyer. The drivers came back on foot with nothing but the story. It will be the carters and the market sellers who go short this week, not the men who signed the papers.

variants.headline: The account of a plundered route
body: Routes lost: one, and it left from our own land.
Gold in the raiders' hands: {{gold}}.
Cargo: gone. The debt for it stays here, and the ledger will show it beside the road that closed.

variants.headline: Trade route to {{destination}} plundered
body: A caravan of ours headed for {{destination}} has been robbed on the road. At the dispatch yard this evening, a merchant is drafting a letter to the buyers who were expecting the load. "They will hear the worst from someone," she says. "Better it comes from us, with an apology and a new date."

variants.headline: Send the spears with the trade
body: Another caravan of ours is gone, {{terms.civic.people}}, and the capital has said nothing about this one. A thief weighs the risk before the profit, and on our roads the risk is nothing. Put spears beside the goods and the price of robbery will rise.

variants.headline: Our trade goes abroad
body: This week carts rolled out of the city loaded for foreign markets. The count of our routes abroad has gone from none to {{routes}}. At the warehouse by the north gate, a keeper has taken the bar off a door that had stayed shut all season.

variants.headline: Hear it! Our trade goes abroad
body: Hear it, {{terms.civic.people}}, hear it! The roads are open and our goods are moving! Our roads abroad now number {{routes}}, and at the last count we had none! Every cart that leaves carries our name with it, and every cart that returns carries our pay!

variants.headline: What a new market can do for one kiln
body: The new trade network has opened roads abroad, {{routes}} in all, and the question worth asking is what they do for a workshop at home. A half-full kiln burns nearly as much fuel as a full one, so a buyer in a foreign town lowers the cost of every bowl fired here. The {{terms.civic.government}} has opened the road; the workshops will do the rest.

variants.headline: The road out stands open
body: A cart that never leaves the yard feeds no one. Send it out and it comes back heavy.

variants.headline: We plunder a foreign trade route
body: Our soldiers have taken a foreign trade route, and its cargo now sits in our depot. A quartermaster spent the afternoon sorting bales stamped with another nation's mark and entering each one in the ledger. The goods will be sold or used, and the road they came by will be empty for a season.

variants.headline: {{gold}} gold taken from a foreign route
body: Our forces stopped a foreign caravan and brought back {{gold}} gold along with the cargo. At the pay table, a clerk is weighing coin that still carries another ruler's stamp. The sum will balance our books this month, and the merchants who lost it will remember the road and the men who took it.

variants.headline: A route from {{origin}} to {{destination}} is plundered
body: Word has reached us that a caravan traveling from {{origin}} to {{destination}} was set upon by our soldiers and brought in with its cargo. That the goods will sell we do not doubt, nor that the officers who took them will be praised for it. We observe only that a great power should take what it means to hold, and a highwayman takes whatever he can carry.

variants.headline: Foreign trade turns a profit
body: They say foreign trade pays a nation slowly, over many seasons. Our soldiers have found a quicker way to collect.

variants.headline: Have we no merchants left?
body: Sir, I have traded across borders since I was young, and I know the names on both ends of every road we use. What our soldiers took was not only cloth and coin, but the promise that a caravan on the road passes unharmed. One day we will want that road open again, and the merchants at the far end will remember who closed it.
